title: Even Rama falls
hookLine: arrows from an empty sky, and Rama, God on earth, falls like a man
carry: the avatar lives a real human life

cards: The first day of fighting goes badly for Lanka. Duel after duel, the monkey and bear leaders win, and the rakshasa champions fall or run. The sun sets, and the fighting goes on in the dark, by the light of weapons.
In one duel, Angada smashes the chariot of Ravana's son, killing his horses and driver. The prince jumps clear. Then he does something the monkeys have no answer for.

teach.b: His name is Indrajit, conqueror of Indra, king of the gods; the epic says he once carried Indra off as a captive. Now he rises out of sight among the clouds and starts shooting.
Valmiki says the arrows turn into serpents as they strike, wrapping Rama and Lakshmana tight, until the two brothers can't move. They fall side by side, covered in shafts.
Sugriva, Hanuman and Jambavan gather around them, stunned. Indrajit shouts down that they're dead, and goes home to tell his father. Stop on that picture, because it's strange.
For Hindus, Rama is Vishnu himself, come down to earth. That's what avatar means: a descent. So how can God lie bound on a battlefield?
The story's answer, as Hindus hear it, is that the descent is real. Rama doesn't pretend to be human; he lives it.

teach.h: I THINK OF MYSELF AS A MAN.
teach.b: At the very end of the war, when the gods come to praise him, Rama says: I think of myself as a man, Rama, son of Dasharatha.

teach.h: GOD GOES ALL THE WAY IN.
teach.b: Many Hindu teachers read that as the heart of the avatar: God doesn't watch a human life from above, he goes all the way in, fear, grief and defeat included. And Valmiki doesn't rush to the rescue.

teach.h: THE AVATAR LIVES A REAL HUMAN LIFE.
teach.b: The first night of the war ends with the heroes down, the sky quiet, and nobody sure whether they're alive. That's why a Hindu can pray to Rama on the worst night of a hard year. He has lain on that field.
A fall doesn't mean God has gone; in this story, God is the one lying there.

how: Ramayana tellers often slow down at the serpent-arrows, the nāgapāśa, letting listeners sit with the heroes' fall before the rescue comes.

o: fire-arrows that Rama rains down on Lanka's walls
serpent-arrows shot from the clouds by Ravana's son
a hail of rocks the monkeys hurl over the gates

games.q: the first night — tap the pairs.

s: Valmiki's Rama announces that he is a god
at the war's end he says, i think of myself as a man, Rama, son of Dasharatha.
Indrajit's name means conqueror of Indra
he once defeated Indra, the king of the gods.
the first night ends with Rama and Lakshmana bound and fallen
Valmiki leaves them there before any rescue comes.

games.q: your little cousin sees a picture of Rama bound by serpents and asks: if rama is God, how did he lose? what fits?
o: as Rama, God lives a real human life, falls and all.
it was a trick; he only pretended to be hurt.
Indrajit was simply stronger than God.
games.why: avatar means descent. Valmiki's Rama says, i think of myself as a man. he truly falls, and truly rises.

practice: When a hard stretch comes, many Hindu families simply say Rama's name, over and over. Sit low and steady, and on each slow out-breath say Ram, softly, picturing the brothers on the field, not yet risen.
If you don't pray, picture them anyway and breathe with them: down, and not alone.

wordCard.voice: Indrajit's arrows. Shot by Ravana's son from out of sight, they bind Rama and Lakshmana, and God on earth falls like a man.

orig.note: Sanskrit avatāra: a descent, from ava, down, and tṛ, to cross: God coming down into the world.

carryVoice: Your line: the avatar lives a real human life. Next, Ravana tries to use the fall against Sita. Day six hundred forty-one, done.
